Bump map explorer

Bump mapping perturbs the surface normal using a texture, so a flat quad is lit as if it were rough. The texture holds a tangent-space normal in RGB (and the height in alpha); the vertex shader puts the light and view vectors into the same tangent space, and the fragment shader does the lighting there. This page combines the bumpMap and bumpMap2 samples and lets you swap the height field, the way it becomes a normal map, the texture parameters, the camera and the light.

Things to try

  • Where the bumps come from. Pick The normal map itself and then Flat surface. The quad is flat in every view; only the normals differ.
  • Light angle. Lower the light's elevation. A raking light shows relief that a head-on light hides. A light below the horizon of the surface lights nothing: the fragment shader zeroes it, which the samples did not do.
  • Normal calculation. Use the raised square at 64 texels and look at its edges. The forward difference makes each edge one texel wide and shifted by half a texel: the left and top edges land just outside the square, the right and bottom edges just inside. The central difference makes edges two texels wide, centred on the true edge. Sobel averages over a 3 × 3 neighbourhood, which smooths noisy height fields.
  • Filtering. Choose the checkerboard, repeat it 8 times, lower the camera elevation and switch the minification filter between NEAREST and LINEAR_MIPMAP_LINEAR. Turn on the mip-level tint to see which levels are used, and try anisotropy.
  • Mipmapped normal maps. generateMipmap averages the encoded normals. The shader renormalizes, but an average of many different normals points in a compromise direction and is shorter than unit length before normalizing, so fine relief fades with distance. That is the right behaviour for a rough surface seen from afar, and it is an approximation.
  • Incomplete textures. Choose a mipmap filter and untick Generate mipmaps. WebGL treats the texture as incomplete and samples black, and the page says so.
  • Perlin noise. The lattice wraps, so the noise tiles without seams; set the wrap mode to REPEAT and repeat 4 times to check, then switch to MIRRORED_REPEAT or CLAMP_TO_EDGE.

Notes on the data: your Honolulu height data is read as 256 × 256 values from 0 to 951 and scaled to 0–1. bumpMap2.js read one row past the end of that array (an undefined value, so NaN normals in the last row); here the edges are wrapped or clamped instead. The normal map is stored as 8-bit RGBA, as in the samples; large bump heights on smooth fields show some banding.
